result.summary: Ovid laments that Cadmus's happiness is undone by his grandson Actæon's fate. Actæon, hunting, stumbles on Diana bathing in the valley of Gargaphie; she turns him into a stag and his own hounds kill him.

scenes.title: Cadmus's prosperity and sorrow
scenes.summary: Ovid reflects that Cadmus seemed happy, but no one is happy before death, and his grandson's fate brought him grief. He argues Actæon's fault was mistake, not crime.

scenes.title: Actæon ends the hunt
scenes.summary: At midday Actæon tells his companions to stop hunting until the next morning.

scenes.title: Diana's grotto and bath
scenes.summary: The valley of Gargaphie holds a natural grotto where Diana bathes, attended by her Nymphs.

scenes.title: Actæon sees Diana
scenes.summary: Actæon wanders in; the Nymphs shriek and shield Diana, who splashes him with water and turns him into a stag, leaving him speechless.
scenes.stakes: Actæon risks the goddess's wrath for seeing her naked, and loses his human form and voice.

scenes.title: Torn apart by his hounds
scenes.summary: Hesitating, the stag Actæon is hunted down by his own pack, unable to speak, while his companions cheer the dogs on. He dies, and Diana's anger is appeased.
scenes.stakes: Actæon's life, as his own hounds pursue and devour him.

alias_notes.explanation: Diana is called Titanian as a descendant of the Titans (Latona's line).
Hyantian means Boeotian, from an old name for the region of Thebes.

notable_quotes.reason: Echoes the ancient saying that no one should be called happy before death.
Diana's taunt cursing Actæon to silence.
Poignant cry Actæon cannot voice as his hounds attack.

analysis.text: Actæon suffers disproportionately for an accidental offense, and Ovid openly calls it a fault of chance, not crime. The tale shows the arbitrary power of gods and fortune.
Loss of voice and human form while retaining human understanding makes the transformation especially cruel.

legacy.text: The Actæon myth became a favorite subject of Renaissance and Baroque painters, notably Titian's Diana and Actaeon (1556–59).

fun_facts.text: Ovid's long catalogue of named hounds has Greek names describing their traits, such as Lælaps (Storm) and Dromas (Runner).

language_notes.text: Cadmus was exiled from Phoenicia while searching for his sister Europa, and founded Thebes; hence 'thy exile'.
Cadmus married Harmonia, daughter of Mars and Venus, so these gods became his parents-in-law.
A proverbial saying, familiar from Solon's maxim that no one should be called happy until dead.
'The horns, too, not his own' refers to the stag's antlers Actæon receives when transformed.
The 'meridian shadow' contracted means shadows are shortest at noon; the sun is midway between east and west.
'Hyantian' means Boeotian, from the old Hyantes tribe of Boeotia, where Thebes lay.
Pumice is light volcanic stone; here it forms the natural arch of the grotto.
'Unstrung bow': a bow was unstrung when not in use to keep it from weakening.
Titanian Goddess: Diana (Greek Artemis) is called Titanian because her mother Latona was a daughter of a Titan. Actæon is Cadmus's grandson, the founder of Thebes.
The comparison concerns the blush of Diana: the red of clouds lit by the sun opposite, or of dawn, is the color of her shame.
Autonoëian hero: Actæon, son of Autonoë, daughter of Cadmus. The epithet recalls his mother's line.
The long list of hounds' names, many Greek words describing traits (e.g. Lælaps 'storm', Theron 'hunter'), is a conventional epic catalogue.
Indolence here means idle slackness; the companions wrongly suppose Actæon is missing the sport out of laziness.
Satiated means fully satisfied; Diana's anger is only appeased by his death.

context_notes.text: Diana (the Greek Artemis) is goddess of hunting, the woods and chastity, attended by virgin Nymphs.
Crocale is a Nymph, daughter of the river Ismenus near Thebes.
Nymphs were female nature spirits who attended Diana, goddess of the hunt and of chastity, and bathed with her in the grotto.
Diana's arrows were her usual weapon; having none at hand, she uses water instead to inflict her punishment.

literary_notes.text: The narrator addresses Cadmus directly, creating sympathy and preparing for the reversal of his fortune.
The horns and the blood-glutted dogs briefly announce the coming transformation and death before the story is told.
Ovid asks what crime a mistake could contain, pleading Actæon's innocence and framing the myth's moral problem.
Nature is given ingenuity and imitates art, suggesting the grotto's perfect, untouched beauty.
Diana's blush is compared to sunlit clouds and dawn, giving the goddess's anger and modesty a vivid, beautiful image.
Actæon cannot cry out at the moment he realizes his state; Diana's curse of silence becomes literally true.
The hunter's familiar paths and his own servants, once instruments of his sport, now become the means of his pursuit.
His mute, kneeling pleas, with looks serving as arms, evoke pity for the helpless victim.
The companions call for Actæon while he stands before them transformed; the reader knows what they cannot.
